item.title: Exercise 2.3.3
item.description:
Let $S_1, S_2, \dots$ be independent exponential random variables with parameters $\lambda_1, \lambda_2, \dots$ respectively. Then:

  • Show that the distribution of $\lambda_1 S_1$ is exponential of parameter $1$.
  • Use the strong law of large numbers to show, first in the special case for $\lambda_n = 1$ for all $n$, and then subject to $\sup_n \lambda_n < \infty$, that $$ \Pr\left( \sum_{n=1}^\infty S_n = \infty \right) = 1 $$ Is the condition that $\sup_n \lambda_n < \infty$ necessary?

item.title: Exercise 2.3.1
item.description:
Suppose $S$ and $T$ are independent exponential random variables of parameters $\alpha$ and $\beta$ respectively.

  • What is the distribution of $\min \{ S, T\}$?
  • What is the probability that $S \leq T$?
  • Show that the two events $\{S \leq T\}$ and $\{\min\{S, T\} \geq t\}$ are independent.

Solution #

  1. For the first problem we use the CDF trick. Concretely, call $Y = \min\{S, T\}$ then: $$ \begin{aligned} \Pr( Y \leq y ) &= 1 - \Pr\left( Y > y \right) \\ &= 1 - \Pr\left( S > y , T > y \right) \\ &= 1 - \Pr(S > y) \Pr(T > y) \\ &= 1 - e^{-\alpha y} e^{-\beta y} \\ &= 1 - e^{-(\alpha + \beta)y} \end{aligned} $$ This is clearly the CDF of an exponential variable $\text{Exp}(\alpha + \beta)$.
